prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "AMGEN INC" (ticker AMGN), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "AMGN", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Amgen Inc.
markets: Cardiovascular and bone health (Repatha, Prolia, Evenity)
Oncology and hematology (Xgeva, Kyprolis, Blincyto, Imdelltra, Nplate, Vectibix, Lumakras)
Obesity and metabolic disease (MariTide in Phase 3)

mission.source: Amgen website, Mission and Values page (amgen.com/about/mission-and-values)
mission.plain: Everything Amgen does is meant to help sick people get better.

about.plain: Amgen is one of the world's biggest biotech companies. It uses living cells to make medicines, often shots, that are very hard to copy. Its medicines lower bad cholesterol, make weak bones stronger, fight cancers and calm immune diseases. It also makes cheaper copies of other companies' biotech drugs and is testing a once-a-month weight-loss shot.
about.customers: Hospitals, clinics, pharmacies and drug wholesalers buy its medicines, mostly paid for by insurers and governments for patients.
about.everyday: If a grandparent gets a twice-a-year shot for thinning bones (Prolia) or a cholesterol shot (Repatha), it is probably made by Amgen.

money.plain: Repatha for cholesterol, Prolia and Evenity for weak bones
Xgeva, Kyprolis, Blincyto, Nplate, Vectibix and new lung-cancer drug Imdelltra
Enbrel for arthritis, Otezla for psoriasis, Tezspire for severe asthma
Tepezza for eye disease, Krystexxa for severe gout, Uplizna and Tavneos
Pavblu (copy of Eylea), Mvasi, Amjevita, Wezlana
MariTide, an obesity drug in nine Phase 3 studies, no sales yet

result.summary: Amgen has a solid but patent-dependent advantage: decades of know-how in making complex biologic medicines at scale, a broad portfolio of 20-plus brands and a global sales machine produced FY2025 revenue of $36,751M, up 10% with 13% volume growth. Its edge is not permanent, as US biosimilars cut Prolia and Xgeva sales by about a third in Q2 2026 and Medicare price setting hit Enbrel, so it must keep replacing older drugs with new ones like Repatha, Evenity, Tezspire, Imdelltra and possibly MariTide.

pricingPower.evidence: FY2025 product sales grew 10% on 13% volume growth offset by 3% lower net selling prices; Enbrel net price fell 36% in FY2025 and 22% in Q2 2026 under IRA Medicare pricing, Prolia net price fell 12% in Q2 2026 after biosimilars, while Tepezza (+6% net price) and Krystexxa still raised prices.

moats.evidence: Patents and regulatory exclusivity on Repatha, Evenity, Tezspire, Tepezza, Blincyto and Imdelltra protect most of its growth, though Prolia/Xgeva (US biosimilars from 2025) and Enbrel show how exclusivity ends.

Doctors and patients stable on a biologic (for example Tepezza or Blincyto protocols) rarely switch, but payers can move patients quickly once cheaper biosimilars arrive, as Prolia's 20% Q2 2026 volume drop shows.
Medicines do not become more valuable as more people use them.

With $36,751M of FY2025 revenue, $7,272M of R&D and large biologics plants in Puerto Rico, Ohio and North Carolina, it can run huge outcome trials (Repatha's VESALIUS-CV) and manufacture at a scale few biotechs match.
Most of its markets have several competitors, such as Regeneron/Sanofi's Praluent and Novartis' Leqvio against Repatha, and Sandoz and Celltrion biosimilars against Prolia.

Its biosimilars business (Pavblu was the only US Eylea biosimilar on the market in Q2 2026) lets it profit from other companies' patent expiries, but rivals like Sandoz and Samsung Bioepis do the same.
Over 40 years Amgen built deep protein-engineering and biologics manufacturing expertise and pioneered bispecific T-cell engagers (Blincyto, Imdelltra), which are hard for new entrants to replicate.
It owns exclusive molecules like MariTide (a monthly obesity antibody-peptide) and its deCODE Genetics human-genetics database in Iceland, but neither guarantees commercial success.

customers.evidence: Physician demand is strong for newer drugs (Repatha +37%, Evenity +38%, Tezspire +42% in Q2 2026, all volume-driven), but payers and patients switch quickly to cheaper versions when exclusivity ends, as with Prolia (-32%) and Xgeva (-34%) in Q2 2026.

talent.evidence: BioSpace lists Amgen as a Best Place to Work every year 2022-2026, and it has appeared on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For; it hired Dana-Farber/Novartis scientist James Bradner as head of R&D in 2023.

product.evidence: Repatha cut cardiovascular events in the FOURIER and VESALIUS-CV outcome trials, Tezspire is the only biologic approved for severe asthma without a phenotype limit, and Imdelltra extended survival in small-cell lung cancer (DeLLphi-304 and DeLLphi-305).

competitors.name: Regeneron Pharmaceuticals
competitors.note: Praluent versus Repatha in PCSK9 cholesterol; Eylea versus Amgen's Pavblu biosimilar; Dupixent versus Tezspire in asthma.

competitors.name: Sandoz Group
competitors.note: Denosumab biosimilars (Jubbonti/Wyost) erode Prolia and Xgeva; competes with Amgen across biosimilars; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: Novartis
competitors.note: Leqvio versus Repatha in cholesterol, Cosentyx versus Otezla in psoriasis, cancer and rare diseases.

competitors.name: Eli Lilly
competitors.note: Zepbound/Mounjaro and orforglipron are the incumbents MariTide must beat in obesity; Taltz versus Otezla in psoriasis.

competitors.name: Novo Nordisk
competitors.note: Wegovy and CagriSema in obesity, the market MariTide targets.

competitors.name: Merck & Co.
competitors.note: Oral PCSK9 inhibitor enlicitide threatens Repatha; Keytruda in oncology.

competitors.name: Sanofi
competitors.note: Praluent outside the US and Dupixent versus Tezspire in asthma and COPD.

competitors.name: Johnson & Johnson
competitors.note: Darzalex and Carvykti versus Kyprolis in multiple myeloma; Tremfya and icotrokinra versus Otezla in psoriasis.

competitors.name: AbbVie
competitors.note: Skyrizi and Rinvoq versus Otezla and Enbrel; Humira versus Amjevita biosimilar.

competitors.name: Bristol Myers Squibb
competitors.note: Sotyktu versus Otezla in psoriasis; multiple myeloma and blood cancers versus Kyprolis and Blincyto.

competitors.name: AstraZeneca
competitors.note: Partner on Tezspire but competes with Fasenra in asthma and with lung-cancer drugs against Imdelltra and Lumakras.

competitors.name: Pfizer
competitors.note: Xeljanz and Velsipity in inflammation, biosimilars, oncology and obesity programs (Metsera).

competitors.name: Celltrion
competitors.note: Biosimilars including denosumab and aflibercept copies against Prolia/Xgeva and Pavblu; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: Samsung Bioepis (Samsung Biologics)
competitors.note: Denosumab, aflibercept, ustekinumab and adalimumab biosimilars; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: Teva Pharmaceutical
competitors.note: Biosimilars and generics competing with Amgen's biosimilar and older products.

threats: US and European denosumab biosimilars eroding Prolia ($4,414M in FY2025) and Xgeva ($2,084M), already down 32% and 34% in Q2 2026
IRA Medicare price setting (Enbrel from January 2026, with Otezla and other drugs at risk) and 340B mix pushing net prices down
MariTide Phase 3 failure or tolerability problems (vomiting rates) in an obesity market already led by Lilly and Novo
Oral PCSK9 drugs (Merck's enlicitide) and siRNA rival Leqvio competing with Repatha, its biggest growth driver
High debt ($57,304M at June 30, 2026) left over from the $27.8B Horizon acquisition, limiting flexibility
A long-running IRS dispute over Puerto Rico profit allocation that could bring a large back-tax bill

ceo.name: Robert A. Bradway
ceo.background: BS in biology from Amherst College and Harvard MBA; former Morgan Stanley health-care investment banker, joined Amgen in 2006 and was CFO and then president and COO before becoming CEO (chairman since 2013)

c1.evidence: Amgen is a leader in biologics and biosimilars, but biotech is no longer an emerging industry; its stake in the fast-growing obesity market (MariTide) is still in Phase 3.

c2.evidence: Doctors choose its drugs for outcome data (Repatha's FOURIER and VESALIUS-CV, Imdelltra's survival benefit), an edge that lasts until patents expire, as Prolia's biosimilar losses in 2025-2026 show.

c3.evidence: Amgen is a famous name in biotech and among investors (a Dow component), but ordinary people know its drugs like Prolia or Enbrel better than the company, and it is not the default leader the way Lilly is in obesity.

c4.evidence: Its mission 'To serve patients' is short and repeated constantly, and work like the deCODE genetics program is purpose-driven, but like other big pharma it is also known for price rises and executive pay drawing congressional questioning in 2020.

c6.evidence: “biotech pioneer, big pharma, reliable, expensive drugs”: people see Amgen as a solid, science-driven biotech veteran, a mostly positive impression tempered by worries about high US drug prices.

c7.evidence: Its markets of heart disease, osteoporosis and cancer grow with ageing populations, and obesity could be a market of over $100B, but 2026 revenue guidance of $38.2-39.4B implies only mid-single-digit growth.

c8.evidence: MariTide could take Amgen into obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart failure and sleep apnea (MARITIME program), and dazodalibep (Sjogren's, positive Phase 3 in Sept 2026) and Tezspire in eosinophilic esophagitis open new markets.

m1.evidence: Bradway pushed early into biosimilars and human genetics (buying deCODE in 2012) and into obesity with MariTide, but his strategy is steady portfolio management rather than a bold new vision.

m2.evidence: Bradway is a former investment banker hired in 2006, a professional manager rather than a founder.

m4.evidence: There is no specific public evidence of a servant-leadership style beyond Amgen's consistent Best Places to Work recognition.

m5.evidence: Amgen has a science-based culture that invented bispecific T-cell engagers (Blincyto, Imdelltra) and MariTide, but much of its growth came from acquisitions (Onyx, Otezla, ChemoCentryx, Horizon).

m6.evidence: Bradway has a biology degree but his career was investment banking and finance, and R&D is led by James Bradner.

m7.evidence: Bradway has a clean personal record and spoke out on racial inequality in 2020, but was questioned in Congress in 2020 over drug prices and executive pay.

m7b.evidence: He gave commencement speeches at UCLA Anderson School of Management (2017) and Keck Graduate Institute (2016), but not at Stanford, Harvard or MIT.

m8b.evidence: Bradway is a low-key, disciplined executive without a celebrity-style public persona.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2012, revenue roughly doubled from $17.3B to $36,751M in FY2025, and he integrated the $27.8B Horizon deal while growing product volume 13% in 2025.

m10.evidence: Amgen is known for disciplined cost control and margins (non-GAAP focus on operating efficiency) but not for Bezos-style frugality.

c10.evidence: Its drugs treat millions of people with heart disease, osteoporosis, cancer and arthritis in about 100 countries, and its early Epogen and Neupogen transformed dialysis and chemotherapy care, but they are costly and mainly reach rich countries.

p2.evidence: Discovering, testing in large outcome trials and manufacturing complex protein medicines like bispecific antibodies is extremely hard and matters for serious diseases.

f2.evidence: Gross margin fell from 75.8% in 2020 to 67.2% in 2025 and operating margin from 35.9% to 24.7%, mostly due to Horizon acquisition amortization.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 debt was $57,304M versus $13,989M of cash and FY2025 operating cash flow of $9,958M, though stockholders' equity was positive at $11,688M.

f4.evidence: Operating income was $9,139M in 2020 and $9,080M in 2025, and operating cash flow of $9,958M in 2025 was below 2024's $11,490M.

v1.evidence: Some products are best-in-class (Repatha with outcome data, Tezspire, Blincyto, Imdelltra), but Amgen as a whole has no single product an ordinary person would pick over every alternative.

v2.evidence: BioSpace has named Amgen a Best Place to Work every year 2022-2026 and it has appeared on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For, but it is not a top-of-list employer like the leading tech firms.

c5.evidence: If Amgen disappeared, millions of patients on Repatha, Prolia, Enbrel, Blincyto or Tepezza, and doctors who rely on them, would have to find substitutes, and some leukemia, lung-cancer and thyroid-eye-disease patients have few alternatives.
